paras: The attempted lynching of Wheeler Kimbro, Walter Stratton and Lorenzo Martin took place at Fremont, Ohio, early on May 10, 1903, when a crowd surrounded the jail demanding the three Black men, who were charged with killing a white man, Otto Mischke, during a strike at the Clauss shear works. Sheriff Mason threatened to shoot the first man who broke in, the crowd dispersed, and the men were later tried, Martin being convicted of manslaughter in 1904. White papers told it as a sheriff's stand against a mob; the Cleveland Gazette argued that the three had fired in self-defense.
According to the Gazette, the three were among Black workers from Cleveland and other northern Ohio towns hired to take strikers' places at the shear works.

Accounts of the shooting late on May 9 differ: the first Fremont wire said party guests leaving the Gummell home met a crowd of "colored men," remarks passed, and the Black men opened fire, killing Mischke, 20, and wounding Albert Gummell. The New York Sun reported instead that Ralph Gommell made a remark and threw a stone that struck Kimbro before the men drew revolvers, and the Gazette said a mob of "strikers and sympathizers" assaulted the three, who fired back in self-defense.

Police arrested the three in a house; the Gazette said it was the house of Richard Pettiford, a shear-works foreman. From about 1 to 4 a.m. a crowd surrounded the jail calling for the prisoners while Mason warned from the steps of his residence that he would shoot anyone who broke down the door. The Sun counted 200 men, one wire said the mob tried several times to get in, and the Gazette called it "a very weak attempt" by "two or three" men. The prisoners were then held at Norwalk, in Huron County, for safe keeping.

Mayor Engler closed the saloons, and Governor Nash refused the sheriff's request for troops. On May 11, the Sun reported, strikers stormed the house of a Black family, and many Black residents left for Oberlin and other places. After the strike was settled on open-shop terms, the three were returned to Fremont on May 16.

The three were bound over without bail for first-degree murder at Bellevue, and Richard Pettiford and his son Will were arrested at Berlin Heights on May 13 while going to give themselves up. On May 18 a grand jury indicted all five for murder, the Pettifords as accessories "in that they were advisers." After a change of venue, Martin was found guilty of manslaughter at Sandusky in February 1904 and was reported sentenced to ten years, pending appeal. Kimbro and Stratton were returned to Sandusky County on a reduced shooting charge and were out on $1,000 bail by June; no report of the Pettifords' cases was found.

Cleveland's Jewett Anti-Lynching League sent attorney Wm. T. Clark to Fremont but refused further spending, even when the men's white Fremont attorneys asked for money. Writing from jail, one prisoner called Mason "a man among men."

White papers ran the wires under headlines on the mob and the sheriff: "Mob Ready With Rope" (Salt Lake Herald), "Was No Lynching" (Savannah Morning News), "Held Mob at Bay" (Alexandria Gazette), "Sheriff Kept Back Ohio Mob Intent on Lynching Negroes" (Louisville Courier-Journal). The text also ran in the Ohio Democrat and, as "Three Negroes Nearly Lynched," in the Fredericksburg Free Lance. The wires gave the party guests' and police account, the Salt Lake Herald calling the prisoners "Negro Murderers"; only the Sun's "Shot in a Race Clash" mentioned the stone.

The Gazette's "The Fremont Riot" set out to give "the truth" a hearing against conflicting stories "sent broadcast," mocked the jail crowd as admirers of "the southern way," and called the Pettifords' charge "foolish." It later wrote that the men would have been lynched by "a second mob" but for Mason, blamed their prompt indictment on local prejudice, and followed the case into June 1904, calling one defense decision "A GREAT MISTAKE."
Who began the violence is disputed: the first wire blamed the Black men, while the Sun and the Gazette, independently, described a white assault first.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Wheeler Kimbro, Walter Stratton and Lorenzo Martin
bases: A crowd surrounded the jail at Fremont demanding three Black prisoners charged with killing a white striker's ally and was held off by the sheriff, an attempted lynching arising from a strike at the Clauss shear works (A1, A3, A5, A12, A14).

No one was killed by the mob: the crowd that demanded the prisoners dispersed after Sheriff Mason threatened to shoot (A3, A5, A14); it was an attempted lynching of men accused of Mischke's killing, by a crowd the Sun put at 200 (A5) and the Gazette at 'two or three' (A14).

The crowd at the jail and the sheriff's stand are reported by the independent Fremont wires (A1, A3), the New York Sun's separate account (A5) and the Cleveland Gazette (A14); who began the street fight is contested (A1 vs A5, A14).

accounts.label: First Fremont wire
accounts.gist: Party guests met a crowd of 'colored men'; remarks passed and the Black men started the shooting, killing Mischke and wounding Gummell; a mob formed and went to the jail.

accounts.label: Second Fremont wire
accounts.gist: The men took offense at Mrs. Gommell's question as to who they were; Mischke was shot coming to the door; Sheriff Mason held off the crowd at the jail.

accounts.label: New York Sun dispatch
accounts.gist: Ralph Gommell made a remark, the men replied, and Gommell threw a stone striking Kimbro; the men then fired; a crowd of 200 demanded them at the jail but dispersed without a leader.

accounts.label: Cleveland Gazette
accounts.gist: A mob of strikers and sympathizers assaulted the three, who fired back in self-defense; the lynching attempt at the jail was weak and ended by the sheriff's threat.

framing.detail: Headlines centered the mob and the sheriff ('Mob Ready With Rope', 'Was No Lynching', 'Sheriff Kept Back Ohio Mob Intent on Lynching Negroes') and called the prisoners 'Negro Murderers', giving the guests' and police version.
The Sun's 'Shot in a Race Clash' reported the thrown stone that struck Kimbro before the shooting.

The Gazette's 'The Fremont Riot' set out to give 'the truth' a hearing, called the shooting self-defense, mocked the jail crowd as admirers of 'the southern way', and called the accessory charge 'foolish'.
Later notes blamed prejudice and sympathy for strikers in Sandusky County for the prompt indictment, praised Sheriff Mason and Ohio's anti-lynching law, and criticized the defense's choices.

record_check.dossier: The mob's targets were Wheeler Kimbro, Walter Stratton and Lorenzo Martin; the Pettifords were arrested days later and indicted as accessories, with no report of a mob against them.
Fremont (shooting and jail crowd); Bellevue was only the site of the preliminary hearing.

record_check.record: accused of being accessories to the murder of Otto Mischke
record_check.dossier: The three targets were charged with murdering Otto Mischke; the accessory charge applied to the Pettiford father and son.
Jail siege (crowd surrounded the jail demanding the prisoners), preceded by a street assault on the three per the Sun and Gazette.
A white crowd at the Fremont jail; the Gazette calls the street assailants strikers and sympathizers.
In custody at the Fremont jail; not taken; moved to the Norwalk jail.
One white man, Otto Mischke, killed in the street shooting that preceded the mob (the three were charged with it); no Black deaths.

record_check.record: A mob assaulted three Afro-American men under arrest at Pettiford's house in Bellevue...
record_check.dossier: The Gazette places the three at Pettiford's house when the mob assaulted them, but nothing places that house in Bellevue; the mob episode was at Fremont.
corroborated: Fremont wires, the Sun and the Gazette.

info: Shooting late on the night of Saturday, May 9, 1903; crowd at the jail from about 1 to 4 a.m. Sunday, May 10
Fremont, Ohio: street near the Gummell/Gommell house, then the jail at Fremont; prisoners then moved to the jail at Norwalk
Wheeler Kimbro (also 'William Kimbro'), Walter Stratton (also 'Charles Stratton'), Lorenzo Martin, Black workers hired at the Clauss shear works in place of strikers
Charged with the murder of Otto Mischke, a white man, and the wounding of Albert Gummell/Gommell; Richard and William Pettiford later indicted as accessories 'in that they were advisers'
A crowd of white Fremont residents at the jail; the Gazette describes the earlier street assailants as 'strikers and sympathizers'
Martin sentenced to ten years, appealed; Kimbro and Stratton returned to Sandusky County to be reindicted on a shooting charge, out on $1,000 bail by June 1904; no outcome for the Pettifords reported
